label: Suicidal Thoughts
framing: If you are thinking of ending your life, your pain is real and it deserves to be taken seriously, but the thought it is telling you, that there is no way through, is lying to you. You are not a burden, you are not beyond help, and the God who made you has not let go of you, even when you have lost your grip on him.
cultural: We live among people who suffer in silence, taught that to admit despair is weakness, and so many carry the darkest thoughts alone, certain no one would understand. Scripture refuses that silence, giving us prophets who asked God to take their lives and a faith that names despair out loud rather than hiding it, because what is spoken can be carried by more than one set of hands.
historical: Elijah, around 850 BC, collapsed under a broom tree and begged God to let him die, and God's answer was not a rebuke but rest, food, and a quiet word. Charles Spurgeon, the most famous preacher of the nineteenth century, spoke openly of a depression so heavy he sometimes wished he had never been born, and he refused to call it unbelief, naming it instead as a real affliction the faithful endure.
application: Right now, if you are in danger, call or text 988, the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, where someone will answer day or night, or go to your nearest emergency room. Tell one person today, out loud, what you are carrying, your pastor, a friend, a doctor, anyone, and do not wait until you feel like it. This is not weakness but the bravest and most faithful thing you can do, and you do not have to survive this alone.

verses.text: And Elijah was afraid and ran for his life. When he came to Beersheba in Judah, he left his servant there, while he himself traveled on a day’s journey into the wilderness. He sat down under a broom tree and prayed that he might die. “I have had enough, LORD,” he said. “Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.”
verses.where: Elijah has just stood against the prophets of Baal, and now the queen has sworn to kill him. Exhausted, afraid and convinced he has failed, he goes alone into the wilderness and asks God to take his life. The Bible sets the prayer down plainly and does not scold him for it.

verses.text: A second time the angel of the LORD returned and touched him, saying, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.”
verses.where: God's answer comes in a striking order. Before any words of correction, an angel touches Elijah and gives him bread and water, and he sleeps. Then a second meal, because what lies ahead is too much for him. Rest, food and company come first.

verses.text: Why is light given to the miserable, and life to the bitter of soul, who long for death that does not come, and search for it like hidden treasure, who rejoice and greatly exult when they can find the grave?
verses.where: After losing his children, his wealth and his health, Job wishes he had never been born and asks why life is given to people in misery. He says it aloud, to God and to his friends. The book keeps his words, and it does not end in chapter 3; his anguish is the beginning of a longer road that leads him to meet God.

verses.text: We do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the hardships we encountered in the province of Asia. We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life. Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead.
verses.where: Paul tells a church that in Asia he was crushed beyond his strength, so that he despaired of life itself. He does not hide it to look strong. He says it taught him to rely on God who raises the dead, and he thanks the church whose prayers helped carry him through.

verses.text: O LORD, the God of my salvation, day and night I cry out before You.
verses.where: Psalm 88 is the one psalm that never turns from complaint to confidence. It ends with darkness as the man's closest companion. And yet it begins by calling God the God of my salvation, and he keeps crying out day and night. Faith here looks like not letting go, even when there is no feeling left.

verses.text: If I say, “Surely the darkness will hide me, and the light become night around me”— even the darkness is not dark to You, but the night shines like the day, for darkness is as light to You.
verses.where: David asks where he could go to get away from God, and every place he names, the heights, the depths, the far side of the sea, God is already there. Even darkness that seems to cover everything is not dark to God.

verses.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.
verses.where: A psalm of thanks for rescue admits that the righteous have many troubles. What it promises is God's nearness to people whose hearts are broken and whose spirits are crushed. It does not say the brokenhearted are failing.

verses.text: A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice.
verses.where: God introduces his chosen servant, whom the Gospels see fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 12:18-21). He will not shout or crush. A reed that is already bent he will not snap, and a wick that is barely smoking he will not put out. He handles what is nearly broken with care.

verses.text: Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!
verses.where: The writer has described his affliction in the bleakest pictures in the book. Then he does something deliberate: he calls to mind what he knows of God's character. Hope begins not as a feeling but as a remembered truth, held on to one morning at a time.

verses.text: For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
verses.where: Paul names everything that might come between a believer and God, trouble, hunger, danger, death and life, the present and the future, and says none of it can separate us from the love of God in Christ. The chapter that began with no condemnation ends with no separation.

links.label: Suffering and the Silence of God

whole: If you are thinking about ending your life, please do not stay alone with it. Tell someone today, a person you trust, a doctor, a pastor, or a crisis line where you live, and if you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Everything below can wait until you have done that.

Thoughts like these are more common than people say, even among people of deep faith. They often come with exhaustion, grief, shame, depression, long pain or a loss that has not been spoken about. They can feel like clear thinking: that the pain will never change, that you are a burden, that others would be better off. Those thoughts are real, and they are heavy. They are not the truth about you. Pain narrows what a person can see, and the narrowing is part of the pain.

The Bible does not pretend that faithful people never feel this. Elijah asked God to take his life. Job wished he had never been born. Paul despaired of life itself. Psalm 88 ends in darkness. What is striking is how God meets them. He does not lecture Elijah; he gives him sleep, bread and company, and only later speaks. He does not condemn Job's cry. He brought Paul through by people who prayed. The God of the Bible is not waiting for you to feel better before he comes near. He is near the brokenhearted now, and he handles a bruised reed without breaking it.

So the wisdom here is simple and urgent. Do the next small thing: tell one person, eat something, sleep, see a doctor, let someone sit with you. Seeing a doctor about this is wise and is not a lack of faith; what lies under these thoughts can often be treated. Let others carry what you cannot, as Paul let the church pray for him. If you can pray, pray honestly, even in the words of Psalm 88. And hold on to what you cannot feel right now: that nothing in all creation, not this darkness and not this night, can separate you from the love of God in Christ Jesus. Your life is not over, and it is not yours alone. Stay.
deep.sit: Who is one person you could tell today, and what is the first sentence you would say to them?

prayer.lead: A prayer of David when his heart was faint. If you have no words of your own, these are enough.
prayer.text: Hear my cry, O God; attend to my prayer. From the ends of the earth I call out to You whenever my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I. For You have been my refuge, a tower of strength against the enemy.

careLines.text: But if darkness feels like your closest companion, please do not carry it alone.
Tell someone you trust today: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
Sorrow that lasts, or that takes away sleep, hope or the wish to go on, is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country.
If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
